This fictional manual is intended to help investigators recognize a scheme, not to encourage securities fraud. A typical manipulator starts with a thinly traded security because a modest amount of activity can make the order book and volume appear more significant than they really are. Before acting, the person accumulates a position through accounts that appear unrelated and selects a period with little independent news or liquidity.

The campaign then creates a false impression of demand. Several accounts place buy orders at progressively higher prices, sometimes cancelling and replacing them so the visible book looks active. Small executions can establish a rising print while larger displayed orders create a sense that more buyers are waiting. At the same time, promoters publish enthusiastic but unsupported claims in chat rooms, newsletters, or social-media posts. The claims are written to sound like independent research, and any financial interest is omitted. New buyers who interpret volume and online excitement as confirmation provide the real liquidity.

Once the price has moved, the original group sells into the increased interest in small pieces rather than one conspicuous block. Some accounts may continue posting optimistic messages while others reduce exposure. After the selling pressure becomes visible, the price can fall quickly because the underlying demand was never broad. The people who arrived late bear most of the loss.

A related pattern uses misleading negative information and short positions: coordinated accounts sell or borrow shares, circulate an unverified rumor, and cover after the price falls. Another uses deceptive orders near a benchmark or market close to influence a reference price. Each pattern leaves different traces in order and communications data.

Investigators compare beneficial ownership, device and funding links, order timing, cancellation behavior, message authorship, and profits across venues. They also examine whether the public claims were false, whether positions were disclosed, and whether the same people traded before and after the messages. A disclaimer does not transform an actionable scheme into lawful conduct.

A responsible exercise should use invented securities, synthetic accounts, and simulated prices. It should end with controls: beneficial-owner aggregation, communications retention, alerts for coordinated timing, review of suspicious promotions, restricted access to confidential information, and prompt escalation to compliance and regulators. Real orders, real rumors, and real targets should never be used for a training drill.
